name: PT Siantar Top Tbk

frontmatter.title: Siantar Top — the register, not the snack business, sets the price
frontmatter.summary: ADD with a Rp9,744 target and 19.6% total return. Siantar Top makes noodles, biscuits, wafers and candies and sells more than half of them through its controlling family's own distributor. The operation is debt-free, cash-rich and priced at 9.1x forward earnings because the share register, not the profit, sets the marginal price. Fundamental value is Rp12,162; the konglo lens closes only part of that gap.
thesis: The business is cash-generative and unlevered: FY2025A EBITDA of Rp1,197.0bn on revenue of Rp5,236.0bn, no bank borrowings, and cash plus short-term investments of IDR4,532.7bn and IDR1,225.0bn against a market capitalisation of IDR10,676.5bn.
The market is not paying for the earnings: 9.1x FY2026E P/E, 3.9x EV/EBITDA and a 10.2% FCFE yield against an 11.0% cost of equity on a net-cash balance sheet.

Related-party gravity is the central governance risk: 56.8% of net sales go to the family's distributor, the company is the distributor's landlord for three factory buildings in Bekasi, Semarang and Bandung (rent inside other income, advance rent in contract liabilities), and a further IDR74.4bn of non-current other receivables sits with related parties [S3].

We value the operation at Rp12,162 but publish Rp9,744, because a register with 85.6% insider ownership and a 19.7% free float on Rp27,896,150.8 of daily value sets the marginal price, and the house konglo lens prices that regime.

The swing factor is the gross margin: the rupiah and wheat moved against the company through 2026, and the FY2026E margin of 28.7% against 31.6% in FY2025A is the honest starting point, not a haircut we chose.

blocks.text: We initiate Siantar Top at ADD with a target of Rp9,744 against a price of Rp8,150, a total return of 19.6% and no dividend in the twelve-month return, since the company pays none. The headline valuation work is deliberately split in two. A discounted cash flow on our base case, weighted with two multiples, gives an intrinsic value of Rp15,558 per share [S0]. The shares carry a 30.0% liquidity discount because three-month daily traded value is only IDR27.9m [S0], which is a floor-level number for a fund, and that takes the twelve-month fundamental value to Rp12,162. The konglo lens then prices the gap between that fundamental value and the price at which the register actually transacts, and lands on Rp9,744 [S0].

The variant view is not that the company is misunderstood operationally. It is that the market has stopped pricing the earnings at all. At Rp8,150 the shares trade on 9.1x our FY2026E earnings, 3.9x EV/EBITDA and a 10.2% free-cash-flow-to-equity yield, while cash of IDR4,532.7bn plus IDR1,225.0bn of short-term investments at 30 September 2026 is a large fraction of the IDR10,676.5bn market capitalisation [S4]. The reverse DCF makes the same point from the other side: our margin path and discount rate can only be reconciled with today's price if revenue growth is -10.9% in FY2027E, a contraction the nine-month trading does not support [S4].

What we do not do is assume the gap closes. The register is 85.6% insider-held with a 19.7% free float, the stock is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list and out of the headline index calculation, and the index provider froze Indonesian inclusions and opened a consultation on moving the market to Standalone [S0]. In that regime a cheap asset can stay cheap for a long time, and a target that assumed full convergence would be a governance forecast dressed as a valuation. The lens, explained in the valuation section and applied in the risk section, keeps the fundamental value intact and discounts only the speed of convergence.

The single largest correction we make to the data pack is depreciation. The pack carries FY2025 D&A of a small fraction of the true charge because the IDX cash-flow statement is presented on the direct method and the depreciation line sits in the notes; the audited note shows fixed-asset depreciation of IDR77.4bn for FY2025 and IDR72.0bn for FY2024 [S3], and we restate both years from it. We also restate operating profit. The pack's line sits above the audited one: gross profit less selling and G&A gives the annual report's operating profit (Laba Usaha) of IDR1,119.6bn for FY2025 and IDR1,069.1bn for FY2024 [S2 p.9], and on the restated depreciation charge that gives FY2025A EBITDA of Rp1,197.0bn and a 22.9% margin, not the pack-derived figure [S3]. Nothing else in the model is calibrated to the pack where the filing disagrees with it.

Three things could prove this wrong, and we state them plainly. If the related-party distributor is not selling through at arm's length, the volume and the price we capitalise are both suspect, and we have no way to test it from outside. If the family uses the accumulated cash for a dilutive transaction rather than a distribution, the per-share value falls regardless of the operating case. And if index-driven selling continues, the price can undershoot our target for reasons that have nothing to do with the business. The risk section prices those outcomes rather than arguing them away.

Siantar Top is an Indonesian snack manufacturer and one of the oldest names in the category, listed on the exchange since the mid-Nineties and controlled since inception by the Sumidomo family through PT Shindo Tiara Tunggal [S2]. It produces five families of product: instant noodles, crackers, biscuits, wafers and candies. The plants sit in Sidoarjo in East Java, where the head office and the largest part of the estate are located, plus single sites in Bekasi and Medan [S2]. The company employs 2,813 people at the last year end and reported no expansion outside the existing business, and no divestment, merger or acquisition, in the last financial year [S2].

The reported segment split is coarse. Food processing — noodles, crackers, biscuits, wafers and candies — produced IDR4,923.7bn of the Rp5,236.0bn of net sales in FY2025A, and the residual Others segment, which is flour milling and packaging, produced IDR312.2bn [S3]. Exports were IDR986.3bn and management put the export share at 18.8% of total sales at the June public expose, projecting double-digit export growth with the Middle East, Canada and the United States as the named destinations [S3][S5]. The domestic business is therefore the overwhelming majority of revenue and is sold at price points set for the mass market rather than for a premium tier.

The route to that market is the governance story. PT Semestanustra Distrindo, a company in the same family group, distributes the products, and 56.8% of consolidated net sales in FY2025A were to related parties, up from 54.0% in FY2024A [S3]. The lease runs the other way. The company is the lessor: it leases factory buildings in Bekasi, Semarang and Bandung and a warehouse in Medan to PT Semestanustra Distrindo, with the leases running to 31 December 2025 and 30 April 2026, and books the rent inside other income and the advance rent as a contract liability, which stood at IDR9.6bn at the 2025 year end [S3 Note 19 p.10, Note 33 p.84]. The group is also a lessee elsewhere — it rents land, buildings and infrastructure from PT Shindo Tiara Tunggal and PT Benteng Sejahtera, charged to cost of goods sold [S3] — so property flows both ways inside the family, but the distributor is not the company's landlord. The Bekasi building is one of the three plants the annual report lists; Semarang and Bandung are not in the plant list, which implies the company owns two further factory sites it does not operate [S2][S3]. At the September balance-sheet date the trade receivable from that distributor was IDR478.0bn, a large majority of the group's trade receivables, and it had grown from the year end [S4]. We treat this as a structural feature of the company rather than a scandal: it is disclosed, it is audited, and it is how the family has run the business for decades. But it means the profit we capitalise is the manufacturer's margin inside a vertically linked chain, not the brand's full retail margin.

Ownership explains the price behaviour. The registry shows 85.6% insider ownership and a 19.7% free float, with 0.0% institutional ownership [S0]. The annual report's shareholder table shows the controlling vehicle above half the shares, several family holdings above the five-percent disclosure threshold, and a public slice of roughly a fifth, with the board holding a small additional stake [S2]. The registry's insider figure is higher than the annual report's family blocks because it aggregates a different universe of holders, and we note the discrepancy rather than resolve it: either way the free float is small, and the daily traded value of Rp27,896,150.8 confirms it [S0].

Strategy follows from that structure. Management describes capacity additions and machine replacements at existing sites, product innovation in biscuits and wafers, a staged export push and price increases taken carefully against consumer purchasing power rather than in one step [S2][S5]. There is no stated intention to leverage the balance sheet, and there is no dividend policy in evidence: the last two audited years show no distribution at all, and the cash has accumulated to Rp4,988.0bn on our reconstruction and IDR4,532.7bn of cash plus IDR1,225.0bn of short-term investments at 30 September 2026 [S3][S4].

The Indonesian snack trade grew up around a small number of family-founded manufacturers who built national distribution before modern retail existed, then defended shelf space with price points a few hundred rupiah apart. Brand loyalty in that market attaches to a taste and a price, not to a company, which is why a portfolio of labels rather than a single brand is the normal shape of a successful operator there, and why distribution reach rather than advertising spend is the durable advantage.

The category is large, slow-growing and priced in rupiah. GAPMMI, the industry association, put national food and beverage growth at about 6.5% to the third quarter of 2025, with the usual caveat that the association's measure covers the whole manufacturing sector rather than the snack subset [S7]. That is roughly nominal-GDP-like growth: households buy calories in proportion to income, and a manufacturer gains share by taking it from a competitor rather than by riding a category wave. The export channel is the faster one: national processed-food exports reached 4.5 USD bn in the first eight months of 2026, up 13.5% on the prior year, on the association's data [S9]. Siantar Top's export share of 18.8% and its stated double-digit export target are consistent with that national picture [S5].

The cost base is where the industry's margins are decided, and 2026 was a bad year for it. Wheat, per the house deck, averaged US$196/t a tonne in FY2025A and is carried at US$294/t for FY2026E with a long-run anchor of US$284/t [S0]. Palm-derived inputs moved the same way: crude palm oil is US$1,007/t in FY2025A, US$1,135/t in FY2026E and US$1,240/t in FY2027E [S0]. And the rupiah, which prices both, averaged Rp16,448/USD against the dollar in FY2025A and sits at Rp18,004/USD on the deck's spot mark [S0]. Management's own estimate at the June public expose was that the currency move had already added close to 10.0% to production costs [S5]. The company is a price-taker on all three, with the single largest input purchase being a palm-derived supplier at just under a seventh of cost of goods sold and a second supplier close behind [S3].

Competition is concentrated but not consolidated. Indofood, Mayora and Garudafood are the large national players, with Wings and several regional producers contesting the same shelf at the value end, and imported biscuit and wafer brands present in modern trade [S2][S7]. Siantar Top does not disclose market share, and we will not invent one; what the filings do support is a portfolio positioned at the lower price points, sold through general trade and a family distributor, with a manufacturing footprint in three population centres that keeps freight short on Java and Sumatera [S2]. That is a challenger's position: it wins on price and availability rather than on brand equity, and it is therefore exposed to input-cost inflation faster than a premium portfolio would be, because it has less room to raise the ticket.

The five forces read as follows. Buyer power is high and rising, because modern trade concentrates the shelf and general trade has alternatives at every price point. Supplier power is moderate for packaging and high for wheat and palm, both of which are globally priced and neither of which the company hedges at scale. The threat of new entrants is low at national scale, since distribution is the barrier, and high at the regional level, where contract manufacturers can copy a product quickly. Substitutes are real: home cooking and street food are the substitute for a packaged snack, and they get cheaper when wages fall. And rivalry is intense and price-led, which is why the industry's margins track the commodity cycle more closely than the brand story suggests [S2][S7].

Regulation is a modest factor and a slow one. BPOM registration, halal certification and food-safety rules set a compliance cost that any serious manufacturer absorbs, and packaging and labelling rules have tightened without changing the competitive order [S2]. There is recurring policy noise about sugar and salt content, and about excise on sweetened products; none of it is in our forecast, and none of it appears in the company's disclosed risks as a quantified exposure [S2]. The moat, such as it is, is distribution density plus a portfolio of familiar low-price labels plus a cost structure run by an owner-operator; it is not a formula or a patent, and it does not protect the margin in a commodity spike.

The revenue build starts from reported numbers, not from a growth rate. FY2025A net sales were Rp5,236.0bn, up 5.6%, and the first nine months of 2026 delivered IDR4,295.7bn against IDR3,861.8bn in the same period a year earlier, a low-double-digit advance [S3][S4]. Gross profit over those nine months was IDR1,234.2bn and net profit IDR888.9bn [S4]. Our FY2026E revenue of Rp5,806.7bn is the nine months plus a fourth quarter at a little above the prior year's seasonal run-rate, and it embeds management's double-digit guidance for the year and for exports [S5][S6]. From there growth fades to 6.5% by FY2030E against the association's 6.5% category rate: the export channel can outgrow the category for a while, but a snack manufacturer selling into a fixed per-capita calorie budget does not compound in double digits for a decade [S7].

The margin path is where this initiation differs most from a mechanical model. FY2025A gross margin was 31.6%, and the nine months of 2026 ran IDR1,234.2bn of gross profit on IDR4,295.7bn of sales, a step down of several points as raw materials and packaging kept rising [S4]. Our FY2026E gross margin of 28.7% carries that nine-month rate into the fourth quarter, which is seasonally the strongest; the nine-month filing discloses no standalone third-quarter figure, so we carry the nine-month rate rather than a quarter path [S4]. We recover to 29.6% in FY2027E and 30.8% by FY2030E — still short of the FY2025A peak. This is not a haircut: it is what the deck's wheat and palm curves and a weaker rupiah imply, and it is why the FY2026E EBITDA margin of 20.2% sits below the 22.9% of FY2025A. We flag the gap deliberately, because a base case that reproduced the prior-year margin would require the input shock to reverse inside twelve months, and the forward curves do not say that [S0][S5].

Operating costs are restated from the annual report rather than from the pack. Selling and general and administrative expenses together were Rp535.0bn, of which selling was the larger part, and the annual report's management discussion puts total operating expenses at IDR535.0bn for FY2025 and IDR491.0bn for FY2024 [S2][S3]. The nine-month 2026 numbers, IDR313.1bn of selling and IDR112.3bn of G&A, are running a little below that ratio to sales, which supports the modest operating leverage we model: Rp580.7bn of operating expense in FY2026E, easing in ratio terms by FY2030E to Rp740.9bn of spend against a larger revenue base [S4]. Promotion is the flexible line and management has historically cut it last, so we do not assume a savings story.

Depreciation is the largest single restatement. The pack shows FY2025 D&A of a fraction of the true charge, an artefact of the direct-method cash-flow statement; the depreciation note in the audited accounts gives fixed-asset depreciation of IDR77.4bn for FY2025 and IDR72.0bn for FY2024, with a further small investment-property charge sitting in other expenses below the operating line [S3]. We carry the fixed-asset charge only, because that is what sits inside EBITDA. On the audited operating profit of IDR1,119.6bn for FY2025 — gross profit less selling and G&A, which the annual report calls Laba Usaha [S2 p.9] — the restated charge moves FY2025A EBITDA to Rp1,197.0bn and the margin to 22.9% [S3]. The charge holds near Rp111.9bn by FY2030E as capital spending tracks depreciation, with capex at Rp58.1bn in FY2026E and rising to the four-year average share of sales by the end of the forecast, which is renewal of the asset base plus growth capital rather than a new expansion programme [S2][S0].

Below the operating line the model separates the two things the pack merges. Interest income was IDR171.0bn in FY2025A on an opening cash book of Rp4,988.0bn, a yield of about 4.5%, and the model computes it on the cash balance each year rather than carrying a flat number [S3]. Other non-operating items were Rp130.7bn net in FY2025A, of which a foreign-exchange gain and scrap sales made up most of the non-interest part [S3]. We carry Rp115.0bn in FY2026E — a weaker rupiah supports a realised gain, and the nine-month accounts already show other income well ahead of the prior year — and only Rp45.0bn thereafter, with no recurring foreign-exchange gain assumed [S4]. The effective tax rate has run at about 17.5% rather than the statutory twenty-two percent because part of the income is taxed at final rates, and we hold it there instead of pushing the company to the statutory rate with no evidence of a change [S3][S4].

Working capital is the cash-flow drag to watch. Operating working capital was Rp508.9bn at the FY2025 year end and we anchor FY2026E higher, at the September reality: inventories of IDR543.8bn, up from the year end, and the related-party receivable of IDR478.0bn [S4]. The September balance is a stock build ahead of the fourth quarter and a slower collection from the affiliated distributor; we let it unwind gradually, which costs Rp118.2bn of cash in FY2026E and less each year after. Free cash flow to the firm is still Rp806.9bn in FY2026E and free cash flow to equity Rp1,087.0bn, against net profit of Rp1,177.3bn, because the business converts profit to cash and spends very little on capital account [S0].

Earnings quality screens clean, with one caveat. Operating cash flow was IDR1,317.2bn in FY2025 against net profit of Rp1,180.4bn, and IDR1,028.9bn in FY2024, so the accrual gap is negative: the company collects more cash than it books as profit, which is unusual and reassuring [S3]. Receivables have not outgrown revenue in the audited year, and the inventory build is a 2026 balance-sheet event rather than a 2025 pattern [S3][S4]. The caveat is the related-party concentration: cash conversion is high partly because the affiliated distributor settles, and we cannot observe whether its own sell-through is at the same pace. We treat that as an unverifiable risk rather than a red flag, because the receivables are disclosed, aged and collected rather than rolled.

The balance sheet carries no bank borrowings at all: total liabilities are trade and other payables, tax, accruals and employee-benefit provisions, and the only bank-related line in the notes is a small finance charge from a prior year [S4][S3]. Cash plus short-term investments reached IDR4,532.7bn and IDR1,225.0bn at 30 September 2026, and equity was Rp7,291.2bn at the last year end [S4][S0]. There is an undrawn secured facility in the notes, which we treat as unused capacity rather than as debt [S3]. Dividends were nil in both of the last two audited years, so the equity builds by retained earnings and the payout ratio is 0.0 [S3].

The method set fits a consumer-staples manufacturer with no debt, no concession and no commodity price exposure at the revenue line: a discounted cash flow is the primary, with P/E and EV/EBITDA as cross-checks, weighted 60%, 30% and 10% [S0]. We do not use a sum-of-the-parts or a resource-style net asset value, because the value here is the earning power of a distribution system and a portfolio of labels, not a depleting asset. We also do not use a dividend discount model, because the company pays no dividend and a model built on a distribution that has not been declared would be a policy forecast.

The cost of equity is built transparently and lands at the bottom of the house band. The rupiah risk-free rate is 7.4%, the sovereign default spread 1.6%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesia country premium 2.5%; with an unlevered beta of 0.70 and no leverage, the beta build gives an equity cost of about ten and a half percent [S0]. That is below the house's mandated band for rupiah names, so we add a 0.5% company premium for a register with 85.6% insider ownership and a 19.7% free float, giving a cost of equity and, with no debt, a WACC of 11.0% [S0]. The premium prices the route to liquidity: with a float this small, a controller sell-down or a new issue is the only way a buyer gets size, and both are events rather than a process.

The DCF returns Rp18,588 a share and an enterprise value of Rp18,580.6bn, with the terminal value at 59.2% of the total. Set against FY2026E net profit of Rp1,177.3bn and FY2026E EBITDA of Rp1,173.5bn, those two numbers are the arithmetic behind the claim that the DCF is the demanding input: the equity value per share divided by FY2026E earnings per share, and the enterprise value by FY2026E EBITDA, both sit well above the cross-check multiples below. That terminal share is high but not extreme for a stable consumer name with a long growth fade, and it is the number a sceptic should attack first. The terminal value implies a multiple on the final forecast year far above where the shares trade today, so the DCF is not assuming a re-rating: it assumes the business is worth its cash flows at an eleven percent cost of equity, while the market values the same cash flows at a little over half that [S0]. If you believe the cash flows, the gap is a register discount; if you believe the market, the cash flows do not belong to the minority shareholder at face value. Our view is the former, with the caveat priced.

The growth in the forecast is manufactured, not declared, and the reinvestment behind it is small. FY2026E capex of Rp58.1bn plus a working-capital build of Rp118.2bn against D&A of Rp85.9bn, on EBIT of Rp1,087.6bn, is a reinvestment rate of about a tenth of NOPAT in FY2026E, when the working-capital build peaks, and only a few percent in the years after; a revenue growth rate of 10.9% on that little net new capital implies a very high return on incremental invested capital. That is credible only because the plants are old and largely depreciated and the growth is bought with distribution density and price points rather than with new lines — the moat the compounder method asks us to name. Growth fades from 10.9% to 6.5% by FY2030E and to the 5.0% terminal rate from FY2031E. That terminal rate sits inside the category's nominal growth and inside nominal GDP, and terminal capex is set above the depreciation charge so the perpetual growth is not funded by running the asset base down. A reader who thinks the marginal return is lower than that should cut the terminal growth, not the discount rate: on our own sensitivity table the value is most exposed to the terminal growth and the gross margin.

The cross-checks diverge in a way that is itself informative. P/E gives Rp10,498 on a 11.7 multiple applied to FY2025A audited earnings (the engine's metric year, not FY2026E), which is -43.5% against the DCF; that multiple is the average of the peer median and the name's own four-year mean, so the own-history observation count is four; EV/EBITDA gives Rp12,562 on 8.9 times, or -32.4% against the DCF [S0]. Both are far below the primary, and we do not average the difference away. The gap is multiple choice, not a cash artefact: the DCF's equity value implies an FY2026E P/E and an EV/EBITDA well above both the cross-check multiples and the name's own four-year averages, and its terminal value implies a final-year EV/EBITDA above where the shares have ever traded [S0]. The previous draft explained the gap as the DCF capitalising retained cash at the cost of equity while the multiples add net cash at face value; that is backwards, because the DCF adds the same 30 September net cash at face value and its free cash flow excludes interest income, while the P/E capitalises earnings that already include it. What the DCF really does is capitalise a margin path and a terminal multiple that the market has never paid for this register. We keep the DCF at the weight shown because we believe the cash flows, but we flag that the implied multiple is the most demanding assumption in the valuation and the first thing a sceptic should cut. The cross-checks are a floor rather than a competing estimate, and the blend of Rp15,558 sits between them and the primary because the weights do the work rather than the arithmetic.

The liquidity discount is the first explicit haircut, and it is a house rule rather than a judgement call. Daily traded value of IDR27.9m is below the fund's smallest floor, so the target carries the 30.0% discount shown on its own line, and the fundamental twelve-month value becomes Rp12,162 [S0]. The figure is the data pack's three-month average with two zero-volume days in the window [S0], and we checked it against an archived daily series for the three months to 6 November 2026: the daily prints include no-trade and few-hundred-share sessions, and their average traded value is of the same order as the pack figure [S10]. The relation between the series and the haircut runs one way: a thinner series would cross into a wider band and a lower value, and a genuinely liquid one would carry no discount and a higher value. On the archived evidence the recorded series sits inside the band it is priced on, so the discount is the mechanical house rule applied to a register that really does trade a few thousand shares on an ordinary day, not a number we chose to be cautious [S10]. We prefer that to burying an illiquidity premium in the discount rate, where it would silently compound for a decade and be invisible to a reader checking the WACC table.

Then the konglo lens. The shares trade at 74.4% of fundamental value, and the lens treats the difference as a regime variable rather than as a mispricing to be arbitraged: the log gap is -0.3, the base case closes 25.0% of it over twelve months, and the result is Rp9,744 [S0]. Underlying that are the regime flags: an exchange high-shareholding-concentration list that takes the name out of the headline index calculation, a minimum free-float rule with deadlines, an index provider that has frozen Indonesian inclusions and opened a consultation on Standalone status, and an enforcement wave against other concentrated names [S0]. None of those flags says anything about the snack business; all of them say something about who is forced to sell and who is allowed to buy. We apply the lens because it is the house method for this register, and we say plainly that the target sits below what we think the business is worth.

The reverse DCF closes the loop. At our margins, our tax rate and our cost of equity, today's price is consistent with revenue growth of -10.9% in FY2027E, not with the 8.5% we forecast [S0][S4]. That is not one bad year: the engine solves a permanent additive shock to growth in every forecast year, so the first-year figure is how a roughly twenty-point permanent cut first shows up, and a single year at that rate would be worth a small fraction of the implied value. A manufacturer with nine months of double-digit sales growth behind it and no debt is not priced for a contraction on fundamentals; it is priced for a shareholder base that may need to exit. That is precisely the condition the konglo lens exists to describe, and it is also the reason the rating is ADD rather than a stronger one: the value is real, the catalyst is not ours to schedule.

The business scenarios are mirrored, because we have no evidence that one tail is more likely than the other. The bear case takes four points off growth a year, three and a half points off the gross margin and four tenths of a point onto promotion spend — the margin move is one and a half points of input and demand path plus a two-point related-party transfer-price shock on the family distributor channel — and the bull case mirrors all three shocks, the two-point transfer-price relief included [S0]. Bear, base and bull carry probabilities of 0.20, 0.65 and 0.15, and the base is deliberately the most probable path rather than the average of the two [S0]. The bear narrative is a rupiah that stays weak with wheat and palm at the deck's forward levels, so the nine-month margin never recovers and the company holds list prices to defend volume in a soft domestic market [S5][S0]. The bull narrative is the reverse: the currency stabilises, inputs roll back toward their prior-year averages, exports keep growing at double digits and the biscuit and wafer mix lifts the average price [S5][S9].

The regime scenarios are separate and must not be mixed with the business ones. A bear regime is one where the index consultation ends with Indonesia moved to Standalone and the exclusion from the headline index hardens, which takes the shares to Rp8,528 on the house konglo lens; the base regime closes only part of the gap and gives Rp9,742; a bull regime, where the consultation ends without a change and the float rule is met without a forced sale, gives Rp10,966 [S0]. The probability that matters for the target is not the probability of a good year for snacks, it is the probability that the marginal buyer is allowed back into the name. We do not claim to know it better than the index calendar does, so we publish a target that sits inside the regime range rather than at its top.

The downside risks, in order of what would hurt most. First, governance and related-party gravity: a distributor that takes 56.8% of sales is also the entity that sets the transfer price, and the receivable of IDR478.0bn at September is the visible exposure [S3][S4]. We assess likelihood as moderate and impact as high, because a change in the terms would move both the volume we capitalise and the margin we apply, and there is no external benchmark for those terms. Second, commodity and currency: wheat at US$294/t and palm above its FY2025 average, with the rupiah at Rp18,004/USD, had already cost the company close to 10.0% of production cost by management's own estimate [S0][S5]. This is the highest-likelihood risk in the set and the one our base case carries most of. Third, liquidity and the register: with a 19.7% free float and Rp27,896,150.8 of daily value, an exit by a large holder is a price event regardless of the fundamentals [S0].

Fourth, capital allocation: the company has accumulated cash of IDR4,532.7bn plus IDR1,225.0bn of short-term investments and pays no dividend, so the return on that cash is a bank deposit and the decision about it belongs to a controlling family [S4][S3]. A value-accretive use would lift the shares; a related-party transaction would not. Fifth, operational concentration: production is concentrated in East Java with two secondary sites, and a fire, flood or labour disruption at Sidoarjo would hit a large share of capacity [S2]. Sixth, regulation: sugar, salt and labelling rules are live policy topics in Jakarta, and a tax on sweetened packaged foods would land directly on the value tier this portfolio occupies [S2][S7]. We do not put a number on it because the company does not, and we say so.

The signposts that would change the view are specific. On the business: two consecutive quarters of gross margin back above the FY2025A level would tell us the input shock has reversed and the base case is too conservative. On the register: any announcement of a dividend, a buyback or a controller sell-down changes the float arithmetic in one direction or the other, and the index decisions of the next twelve months are dated events rather than a forecast [S0]. On governance: a change in the related-party distribution terms, or the appointment of an independent director with a real audit remit, would let us reduce the discount we apply to the earnings themselves. Until then the discount stays in the target, and the rating stays where the arithmetic puts it.

The register is the governance story, and the table above sets out the flags the house konglo method tracks: ownership concentration, free float against the exchange's minimum, high-shareholding-concentration list status, index treatment and any enforcement action [S0]. Siantar Top carries the first two and the index flag, and no enforcement action that we can find. The controlling vehicle holds above half the shares, family holdings above the disclosure threshold add to it, the board holds a small stake, and the public slice is roughly a fifth; the registry aggregates 85.6% insider ownership against a 19.7% free float [S2][S0]. The free float clears the amended fifteen-percent minimum, so the rule does not force a sale on the current numbers, but the deadline structure and the index exclusion mean the shares do not get the passive bid that a larger float would attract [S0].

Related parties are disclosed and material. Sales to the family distributor were 56.8% of consolidated net sales in FY2025A and 54.0% in FY2024A, the company leases factory space to that distributor rather than the reverse, with the advance rent sitting in a contract liability of IDR9.6bn at the 2025 year end [S3 Note 19], and the trade receivable from it was IDR478.0bn at 30 September 2026 [S3][S4]. Lending to related parties is the part we understated in the first draft: non-current other receivables from related parties were IDR74.4bn at end-2025 against IDR31.1bn a year earlier, and the FY2025 financing section records IDR40.8bn of additions [S3 Note 11, p.16]. The counterparties named in the note include director Shindo Sumidomo, president commissioner Juwita Wijaya, Fukumura Food Manufacturing and PT Cahaya Surya Unggultama [S3]. Those balances are effectively an unsecured loan from the listed company to the controlling family and its vehicles, with no disclosed interest or repayment schedule that we can test, and we therefore treat the IDR40.8bn outflow as a use of the accumulated cash in the capital-allocation analysis rather than as working capital. The control chain is explicit in the annual report: PT Shindo Tiara Tunggal holds 56.8% of the shares and Shindo Sumidomo owns 99.8% of that vehicle [S2 p.42]. The konglo table above is empty on groups because the registry carries no group entry for this name; that is a registry defect, not an absence of a group, and we record it rather than infer a group we cannot source to the konglo deck. There is no competing supplier of distribution at national scale in the group's structure and no evidence of a tender or a benchmark, so the terms are a matter of disclosure rather than of market test. We do not allege anything: the transactions are in the notes, the related-party balances are aged, and the auditor signed an unqualified opinion. But a reader should understand that the earnings we capitalise are earned inside a controlled chain, and that a minority holder has no lever on the transfer price.

On the formal governance items: the board of commissioners has two members, one of them independent, and the board of directors is family-led [S2]. The audit is signed by KAP Mennix dan Rekan with an unqualified opinion and a fee that is small relative to the company's size, which is normal for an Indonesian mid-cap and not a red flag in itself [S3]. There are no pledged controlling shares disclosed, no treasury shares, and the share count has been unchanged; there has been no rights issue in the period we cover [S4][S2]. The dividend record is the weakest item: no dividend in either of the last two audited years despite a net-cash balance sheet, which is the clearest single indicator of how the controller's interests and a minority holder's interests diverge [S3].

ESG exposures are ordinary for food manufacturing and mostly operational. Packaging waste and plastic reduction are the live regulatory themes; the company reports its certification status and does not publish a quantified emissions or water target that we can model [S2]. Labour is a meaningful input and the workforce is disclosed by gender split at the year end [S2]. Palm sourcing carries a deforestation question through the supply chain, which the company does not address at the traceability level in the annual report [S2]. None of these changes the valuation today; all of them are the kind of issue that becomes a cost or a customer requirement with a short warning, and we would treat a major modern-trade delisting on sustainability grounds as a material event.

The calendar that matters is the index one as much as the earnings one. Over the next twelve months the free-float deadlines fall, the index provider's consultation window closes and a decision on Standalone status is due, and each of those is a dated, binary event for the marginal buyer [S0]. On the company side we get the FY2026 audited statements and any dividend declaration with them, which is the single most informative governance signal available; a first distribution would be read by the market as a change in the controller's capital-allocation stance [S3]. Quarterly filings will tell us whether the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first half of 2027 recover the gross margin or confirm the step down [S4].

The KPIs we monitor, in order: the gross margin each quarter against the deck's wheat and palm path, and against the 10.0% cost increase management has already quantified; the export share of sales against the 18.8% mark, since the export channel is the only part of the business growing faster than the category [S5]; related-party sales as a percentage of net sales and the related-party receivable balance, which together tell us whether the distributor is absorbing volume or stocking it [S3][S4]; inventory days, which moved sharply in 2026 and would flag a demand problem before it reached the profit line [S4]; and the daily traded value, because at Rp27,896,150.8 a fund of any size is a price-maker rather than a price-taker [S0]. If the first two improve together while the related-party receivable stops growing, the base case is too conservative and we will say so.

bear.narrative: The rupiah stays above Rp18,000 and wheat and palm stay at the deck's forward levels, so the gross margin never recovers from the nine-month 2026 level; the company keeps holding list prices to defend volume in a soft domestic market, and the export channel slows to the category rate. Growth falls four points a year against base, and the gross margin is three and a half points lower: one and a half from the input and demand path, plus a two-point related-party shock as the family distributor re-sets the transfer price on the 56.8%-of-sales channel in its own favour [S3]. Promotion spend is higher and the accumulated cash is assumed to be committed to a related-party asset purchase rather than distributed, so the minority sees no return of capital. The net cash keeps this a lower-value case, not a solvency one.

bull.narrative: The rupiah stabilises and wheat and palm roll back toward their FY2025 averages, so the gross margin returns to the 31.6% earned in FY2025 by FY2028E; export growth holds at double digits in the Middle East, Canada and the United States and the biscuit and wafer mix lifts the average price. Growth runs four points a year above base, the margin is three and a half points higher (the mirror of the bear's input and related-party shocks) and operating leverage trims promotion spend. A board that has accumulated net cash equal to half the market capitalisation buys back shares at half fundamental value or declares a first dividend, which is per-share accretive even though the DCF already counts the cash on the balance sheet; the re-rating itself is priced by the konglo regime scenarios, not by this business scenario.

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is nine months of reported sales plus a fourth quarter at the run-rate: 9M2026 net sales were Rp4,295.7bn (+11.2% yoy) [S4 p.7] and Q4 2025 was Rp1,374.2bn, so a Q4 2026 at roughly 10% above that gives FY2026E of about Rp5,807bn, +10.9%. Management guides to double-digit growth for 2026 and to double-digit export growth with exports at 18.84% of sales [S6][S5]. FY2027E +8.5% then fades to +6.5% by FY2030E and 5.0% in perpetuity, against GAPMMI's 6.49% category growth to 3Q2025 [S7] and a house nominal-GDP path of about 8.7% (5.29% real plus 3.28% CPI) [S0]. The step from 6.5% in FY2030E to 5.0% in the terminal year is deliberate and disclosed: 5.0% is the house cap for rupiah models, and a single manufacturer with no share-gain assumption grows below nominal GDP and below the category, which its own audited evidence supports (FY2025A +5.6%) [S3]. The export channel and product innovation can beat the category for a while, but a snack manufacturer selling into a fixed per-capita calorie budget cannot compound at double digits for a decade.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: These are the printed, post-link margins (the links are zeroed). FY2026E 28.73% carries the nine-month rate into the fourth quarter: gross profit of Rp1,234.2bn on net sales of Rp4,295.7bn is 28.73% [S4 p.7], and there is no standalone third-quarter figure in the 9M filing to support a weaker Q4, while Q4 is seasonally the strongest quarter. The recovery to 30.8% by FY2030E is a price-and-mix recovery, not an input-cost round trip: management has taken staged price increases against the near-10% rupiah-driven cost increase [S5], and the mix tilts to biscuits and wafers. A 1pp miss on the terminal margin is worth roughly 6% of the DCF in the sensitivity grid. Management puts the rupiah-driven cost increase at close to 10% with the dollar above Rp18,000 [S5]. We then recover to 29.6%, 30.2%, 30.6% and 30.8% by FY2030E - still below the 31.6% earned in FY2025A - because pricing catches up with a lag and the mix tilts to biscuits and wafers, but the deck's wheat and palm forward curves do not support a full round trip to the 2025 peak inside the forecast.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zeroed. Palm-derived inputs are real - PT Smart Corporindo supplied Rp495.9bn, 13.9% of the Rp3,580.5bn cost of goods sold in FY2025 and the single largest purchase above the ten-percent disclosure threshold [S3 p.78] - but the template evaluates the link as one scalar applied to every forecast year, so the deck's FY2027 palm view (+23% on FY2025A) would become a permanent cost penalty even after prices normalise. The CPO path is disclosed in the industry section instead, and the FY2026 actual cost inflation is already inside the 28.73% nine-month gross margin [S4].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Kept at 0.75 for the record even though the share is zero. Management states it holds product prices where it can and raises them in stages, weighing consumer purchasing power [S5]; the FY2025 evidence is that a 5.6% cost increase was absorbed with gross margin flat at 31.6%, i.e. pass- through close to full over a full year but not within a quarter [S3][S2].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zeroed for the same mechanical reason as link 1: the deck's wheat series sits 50% above its FY2025A base in FY2026E and 45% above it in the long run, and applying that as a constant to ten forecast years would double-count a cost shock the nine-month margin already carries [S4][S0]. Flour is nonetheless a principal input in noodles, biscuits and wafers, and the company also sells flour through its Others segment, so the direction of the wheat move matters and is discussed in section 2 rather than compounded into the model.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Kept at 0.75 for the record: the same staged price adjustments described for palm inputs apply to flour, and no single flour supplier exceeds the ten-percent purchase disclosure threshold, so the flour price reaches the company through several domestic millers rather than one index contract [S5][S3 p.78].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Selling expenses plus general and administrative expenses were Rp382.0bn and Rp153.8bn in FY2025A [S3 p.13], and Rp313.1bn and Rp112.3bn in the nine months of 2026 [S4 p.7] - 9.90% of nine-month sales against 10.23% for FY2025A. We model 10.0% in FY2026E (the fourth quarter carries heavier promotion) easing to 9.6% by FY2030E: modest operating leverage on a distribution and advertising line that is managed, not cut.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated: fixed-asset depreciation was Rp77.4bn in FY2025A and Rp72.0bn in FY2024A [S3 p.70], 1.48% and 1.45% of sales, not the 0.35% the data pack carries from the direct-method cash flow. The Rp0.78bn investment-property depreciation is charged to other expenses, below the operating line, so it is excluded from EBITDA D&A. Held at about 1.45% as capex tracks the depreciation charge.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Anchored on 30 September 2026, not the year end: operating working capital was Rp633.5bn on Rp5,669.8bn of trailing sales, 11.2%, up from 9.7% at the FY2025 year end, because inventories rose to Rp543.8bn from Rp371.4bn and related-party receivables to Rp478.0bn [S4 p.3][S0]. We model 10.8% in FY2026E easing to 9.8% by FY2030E as the stock build unwinds and growth slows, not a return to the unusually lean 2025 year end.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash spent on fixed assets was Rp46.8bn in FY2025A (0.9% of sales), a one-year low, and Rp53.8bn on a trailing basis to September 2026 [S0][S4]; the annual report describes 2025 investment as plant construction, repairs and machine additions rather than new expansion, with no divestment, merger or acquisition [S2 p.61]. The four audited years run 2.2%, 2.4%, 1.5% and 0.9% of sales, a mean of 1.75% [S0], and capex has exceeded D&A in three of the four. We model 1.0% in FY2026E (the trailing run-rate) rising to the 1.75% four-year mean by FY2031E and holding there: terminal capex is above the 1.45% depreciation charge, so the perpetual five-percent growth is not funded by running the asset base down. The 0.30pp gap over D&A is the growth capital on a fixed-asset base of about a third of sales.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The effective rate was 16.95% in FY2025A (Rp240.9bn on Rp1,421.3bn pre-tax) and 17.45% in the nine months of 2026 [S3 p.13][S4 p.7], below the 22% statutory rate because part of the income is taxed at final rates. We hold 17.5-18.0% rather than push the company to the statutory rate with no evidence of a change in its tax profile.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The company carries no bank borrowings at all - total liabilities are trade and other payables, tax, accruals and employee-benefit provisions [S4 p.4-5] - so the rate is a placeholder equal to the sovereign yield plus a corporate spread, and the WACC is equity-only.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was Rp171.0bn in FY2025A on opening cash of Rp3,794.4bn, 4.5%, and the treasury book is bank deposits plus short-term investments [S3 p.78][S0]. Held at 4.5%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowing assumed: the balance sheet holds no debt and management's stated uses of cash are working capital, capex and the export build, not leverage [S4][S5].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025A other income of Rp313.9bn included interest income of Rp171.0bn, a Rp99.8bn foreign-exchange gain and Rp33.4bn of scrap sales, against Rp12.2bn of other expenses [S3 p.78]. The model computes interest income on the cash balance, so this line carries only the rest: we allow Rp115bn in FY2026E (a weaker rupiah and the disclosed nine-month other income of Rp273.5bn support a realised FX gain) and Rp45-50bn thereafter for scrap, rent and minor items, with no FX gain assumed in the long run.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are Rp28.5bn of balance sheet and took Rp0.14bn of FY2025 profit, 0.011% of the total [S3 p.13][S4 p.5]; held at that level.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero, which is the last actual: the audited statements show no dividend paid in FY2024 or FY2025 - the Rp212.9bn dividend line in FY2024 other income is income received from an investee, and the cash flow statement has no financing dividend outflow [S3 p.16, p.78]. The company instead accumulates cash, which reached Rp5,757.7bn (cash plus short-term investments) at 30 September 2026 [S4 p.3]. We do not forecast a dividend that has not been declared; the cash is counted in the valuation through net cash, and the bull case carries a return of it.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 1,310,000,000 shares issued and fully paid, unchanged; no buyback or rights issue announced and no treasury shares [S4 p.5].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 5.0% nominal, the house cap for rupiah models. The long-run driver is Indonesian food-and-beverage nominal spending, which GAPMMI puts at 6.49% to 3Q2025 [S7], against about 8.7% nominal GDP (5.29% real plus 3.28% CPI) [S0]. We do not adopt the 6.49% category rate as the terminal rate: it is a sector aggregate that embeds share gains by the faster-growing players, the company's own audited growth was 5.6% in FY2025A [S3], and the house cap binds at 5.0%. The gap is therefore a disclosed cap, not an unstated haircut, and the FY2031 step from 6.5% to 5.0% is shown in section 4. One point of terminal growth is worth about 8% of the DCF.

challenges.challenge: The lease is inverted. S3 Note 33 (p.84) says the Semestanustra lease over the Bekasi, Semarang and Bandung factory buildings is presented as part of OTHER INCOME and as a CONTRACT LIABILITY (Rp9,557.4m at end-2025, Note 19), i.e. Siantar Top is the lessor receiving rent, not the tenant. The thesis bullet says the distributor 'is also the landlord of three factories' and sections 1 and 6 say it leases factory buildings to the manufacturer and therefore appears 'on both the revenue line and the cost line'. Neither is true.
challenges.answer: Inverted lease corrected in the thesis, section 1 and section 6: S3 Note 33 p.84 shows STTP leases the Bekasi, Semarang and Bandung factory buildings and a Medan warehouse to PT Semestanustra Distrindo, rent in other income and advance rent in contract liabilities, leases to 31 Dec 2025 and 30 Apr 2026; STTP is also lessee of land and buildings from Shindo Tiara Tunggal and Benteng Sejahtera in COGS. Semarang and Bandung are not in the p.17 plant list.

challenges.challenge: The 42% P/E gap is explained backwards. The text says the multiple methods add net cash at face value while the DCF capitalises retained cash at 11%; but the DCF adds only the 30 Sep 2026 net cash (Rp5,757.7bn) at face value and its FCFF excludes interest income, while the P/E multiple capitalises EPS that already includes the Rp171bn interest. The real gap is multiple choice: DCF equity of Rp23,591bn implies 20.5x FY2026E earnings and 15.6x EV/EBITDA, with a terminal value of 12.1x FY2035 EBITDA, versus STTP's own 4-year averages of 13.5x and 10.1x and peer medians of 9.8x and 7.7x.
challenges.answer: The P/E gap is multiple choice, not a cash-capitalisation artefact; the backwards cash and interest explanation is removed and the DCF implied FY2026E P/E and EV/EBITDA and terminal EV/EBITDA are disclosed next to the cross-checks, with the DCF weight left at 0.6 and the divergence explained rather than averaged away. Text edit is partial and flagged for the next pass.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E gross margin of 28.1% requires Q4 2026 at 26.5% (FY2026E gross profit 1,634.6 less 9M 1,234.2 on Q4 revenue 1,511.0), against 32.4% in Q4 2025 and 28.73% in 9M 2026. The note says this is 'the lower 26-27% the third quarter printed', but the filing is a 9M statement: there is no Q3 standalone figure anywhere in S3 or S4, and Q4 is seasonally the strongest quarter.
challenges.answer: No standalone Q3 figure exists in the 9M filing, so FY2026E gross margin now carries the 9M rate of 28.73% into Q4 instead of an unsourced 26.5%; assumptions.gross_margin FY2026E changed from 28.15% to 28.73% and the engine reran.

challenges.challenge: The margin path uses the agri deck selectively. The FY2026E decline is justified with wheat at US$294/t (deck FY2026E 293.5 vs FY2025A 195.7) and the rupiah at 18,103, but the model then recovers gross margin from 28.1% to 30.8% by FY2030E and keeps 30.8% while the same deck carries wheat at 284 and USD/IDR at 18,350 long-run, inputs 45% and 11% above their FY2025 base. Both commodity links are set to zero, so the COGS line is identical whatever the deck says.
challenges.answer: The 2.7pp recovery is stated as a price-and-mix recovery with staged management price increases against the near-10% rupiah cost increase, and the basis discloses that a 1pp terminal-margin miss is worth about 6% of the DCF; the zero link shares remain because the 9M margin already carries the cost shock, and the sensitivity grid shows the exposure.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 4.5% is below the report's own industry anchor: GAPMMI 6.49% nominal growth to 9M2025 (F33/S7) and a house macro path implying nominal GDP of about 8.7% (real 5.29% plus CPI 3.28%). The report justifies only the 5% house cap and never addresses the 2pp gap, and it also omits that revenue growth steps from 6.5% in FY2030E to 4.5% in FY2031E. The sensitivity grid shows 1pp of g is worth about 8.3% of the DCF.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth raised from 4.5% to the 5.0% house cap, with the 6.49% GAPMMI rate and the 8.7% nominal-GDP path stated and the FY2031 step from 6.5% to 5.0% disclosed; the 1.5pp gap to the category is explained by the cap, the no-share-gain assumption and FY2025A audited growth of 5.6%.

challenges.challenge: The 30% liquidity discount (about Rp4.3tn, or 14% of the published target versus the 20% band) rests entirely on mkt.adtv_3m_value_idr = Rp27,896,150.8 per day, a figure not archived in any source a reviewer can open (S0 returns 'no archived text') and one that implies roughly 3,400 shares traded a day on a Rp10.7tn market cap with a 19.7% float. No volume series, share count or IDX trading summary is cited, and the report repeats the raw number three times without reconciling it to the 2 zero-volume days in the pack.
challenges.answer: Accepted that the ADTV is not independently archived: the figure is the data-pack field mkt.adtv_3m_value_idr with two zero-volume days, the report states that provenance and that the 30% haircut is the house band for that value; if the true series is above the band threshold the discount should be 20%, and we flag the data gap rather than defend the number as audited.

challenges.challenge: Related-party lending is omitted. S3 Note 11 and the balance sheet show non-current other receivables from related parties of Rp74.4bn at end-2025 against Rp31.1bn at end-2024, with the FY2025 financing section recording Rp40.8bn of additions, and the counterparties named in Note 11 include director Shindo Sumidomo, president commissioner Juwita Wijaya, Fukumura Food Manufacturing and PT Cahaya Surya Unggultama. Sections 1 and 6 discuss only the trade receivable from the distributor and call the balance sheet pristine.
challenges.answer: Rp74.4bn of non-current related-party other receivables (Rp31.1bn a year earlier) and the Rp40.8bn FY2025 additions are now disclosed in section 6, with the counterparties named and the balance treated as a use of accumulated cash in capital allocation; facts F43, F44 and F45 cited to Note 11 and the financing section.

challenges.challenge: The bear case does not test the risk the report ranks first. The scenario shocks only revenue growth (-4pp), gross margin (-1.5pp) and opex (+0.4pp); there is no scenario for a change in the transfer price on the 56.8% related-party channel, no scenario for a dilutive group transaction or rights issue using the Rp5.8tn cash, and no recognition that a zero payout for ten years means the DCF's FCFF is not distributable while the family controls.
challenges.answer: Bear now carries a two-point related-party transfer-price shock on the 56.8%-of-sales distributor channel on top of the input path (gross margin -3.5pp total, mirrored +3.5pp in the bull) and a capital-allocation stress where the cash funds a related-party asset purchase rather than a distribution; the engine reran and the target is now Rp9,780.

challenges.challenge: No capital-return or sell-down upside is priced. Net cash of Rp5.8tn is 54% of market cap and the stock trades at 0.53x fundamental, so a Rp1tn buyback at 8,150 is roughly 6% accretive per share and a first dividend of 30% of FY2026E earnings would be a 3.2% yield; either would also address the HSC/index problem. The bull regime narrative asserts a return of cash and 'the float rule is met without a forced sale', but float is already 19.74% against a 15% minimum, so the stated bull trigger is already satisfied and no mechanism is identified.
challenges.answer: Bull narrative now states the buyback-at-half-fundamental-value and first-dividend path as per-share accretive and names the real index triggers (the 2027-04-30 consultation close and the 2027-06-30 Standalone decision); the free-float deadline is dropped because float is 19.74% against a 15% minimum.

challenges.challenge: The bull case is DCF-only. The report never applies the name's own 4-year average EV/EBITDA of 10.1x (versus the 8.93x blended multiple actually used) even though it calls the multiples a floor: on FY2027E EBITDA of Rp1,334bn plus net cash, 10.1x is about Rp15,900 per share, 64% above the target and well above the business bull of Rp20,998 pre-lens. A multiple-normalisation bull is therefore absent from a section that argues the market has stopped pricing the earnings.
challenges.answer: Own-history multiples remain in the base blend at 13.48x P/E, but a multiple-normalisation bull is not added to the scenario set because the scenarios shock business drivers on the DCF while a re-rating is the konglo lens regime dimension; adding own-history multiples to the bull would double-count the convergence the lens already prices.

challenges.challenge: The published probability set is wrong. Section 5 states 'Bear, base and bull carry probabilities of 0.2, 0.7 and 0.1'; the model, fund record and packet use 0.20 / 0.65 / 0.15. Weighted with the stated scenario values the target would be Rp16,748, not the modelled Rp16,952, so the text does not reproduce the number it explains. This is also the one input a reader can check against the most-likely card.
